summary: This RFC specifies an application-layer protocol for Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) that passes RID messages over HTTP with TLS. RID messages extend the IODEF XML format used for sharing incident information.

eli5.summary: Security alert notes get sent through the same safe postal route as web pages, so only the right parties can read them.

questions: how are rid messages sent over http
what is the rid callback token
subtitle: How RID incident messages are carried between peers as HTTP requests over mutually authenticated TLS.

tldr.problem: RID messages need an interoperable protocol for moving them between members of a consortium, but IODEF only defines a document format and leaves sharing out of scope.
tldr.mechanism: Each RID system acts as both an HTTP/TLS client and server. Messages are sent with HTTP POST to the path / on TCP port 4590, protected by TLS 1.1 or higher with certificates on both sides, and slow replies use a 202 Accepted callback.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6546 obsoletes RFC 6046, which moves to Historic. It makes the transport a Standards Track document and adds the RID-Callback-Token header.

today: RFC 6546 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2012 that obsoletes RFC 6046, which it moves to Historic status. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the transport used by RFC 6545.

sections.title: Why a Transport for RID
sections.content:
IODEF (RFC 5070) defines a message format, not a protocol, so sharing the messages is out of scope. Real-time Inter-network Defense (RFC 6545) does need a protocol, so that members of a RID consortium interoperate. This RFC supplies one: RID messages travel in HTTP Request and Response messages over TLS, called HTTP/TLS.

Any IODEF message can also use this transport, by sending it as a RID Report message. Only Section 3 is normative: systems must fully implement it to interoperate within a consortium, and the rest is background.
sections.eli5: RID says what the alert note looks like. This RFC says how to mail it: the same kind of safe, sealed delivery that web browsers use.

sections.title: Sending Messages with HTTP POST
sections.content:
Every RID system is both an HTTP/TLS server and an HTTP/TLS client, because it must accept connections from any peer to support callbacks. The RFC admits that HTTP/TLS is not ideal, since HTTP is client-server and RID is message exchange, but ease of implementation outweighs this.

  • RID systems implement all required HTTP/1.1 functionality and SHOULD listen on TCP port 4590. They SHOULD NOT use port 443, so ordinary HTTPS servers are not mistaken for RID systems.
  • Every RID message is sent with POST to the Request-URI /, and the Content-type of requests and responses MUST be text/xml.
  • GET / and HEAD / have no meaning and SHOULD be answered with 204 No Content. Other URIs SHOULD return 404 Not Found.
  • Sending a RID message is idempotent, so a system interrupted during transport MAY simply repeat the transaction.

RID systems MUST support HTTP/1.1 persistent connections (and SHOULD use them) and MUST support chunked transfer encoding on the server side. For security they SHOULD NOT return or follow 3xx redirects, and the protocol has no in-band way to announce a changed address; stable DNS names are RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Every alert goes to the same mailbox number, on a special door (port 4590) instead of the normal web door. The sender can just resend if the first try is interrupted, because repeating a note does no harm.

sections.title: Replies, Callbacks and Error Handling
sections.content:
Queries and replies can be far apart in time, so the receiver MAY answer with 202 Accepted instead of a RID message. This is a RID callback: it has an empty body and a RID-Callback-Token header holding a unique token, an opaque string of up to 255 printable ASCII characters (1*255(VCHAR)). The token must be unique among all callbacks from that receiver to that sender, with no upper time bound.

When it later has the answer, the responder MUST connect to the host at the network address the original request came from, normally on port 4590. There is no redirected callback. A reply SHOULD come in the HTTP Response if ready within about thirty seconds, but RID systems MUST be prepared for a 202, an empty body, a closed connection and a later callback.

Table 1 of the RFC lists which RID types may appear in a response to each request type. For example, an InvestigationRequest or TraceRequest may get an Acknowledgement, Result or Report with 200, or an empty 202; a Query may get an Acknowledgement or Report; Acknowledgement and Result messages, which are sent as callbacks, get an empty 200. A system MUST NOT send any RID message in a response other than the corresponding allowed one.

An improper RID message in a request earns a 4xx result, and a local processing problem earns a 5xx. Because HTTP cannot signal a bad response body, a bad RID message in a response MUST be logged and shown to the administrator.
sections.eli5: If the answer will take a while, the receiver hands back a claim ticket (the token). Later it knocks on the sender's door and says "here is the answer for ticket number so-and-so."

sections.title: TLS and Mutual Authentication
sections.content:
RID systems MUST use TLS 1.1 or higher for confidentiality, identification and authentication, and SHOULD support TLS 1.2. They MUST NOT request, offer or use any version of SSL or any TLS version before 1.1, because of known vulnerabilities. Sessions MUST use non-NULL ciphersuites for authentication, integrity and confidentiality.

Mutual authentication is required: both the HTTPS client and the HTTPS server MUST be identified by an X.509 certificate, with full path validation on each (RFC 5280). Systems SHOULD be identified by a certificate with a DNS-ID as in RFC 6125, using a CN-ID is NOT RECOMMENDED, and wildcards MUST NOT appear in the identifier.

RID systems MUST support checking certificates against an explicit whitelist of peer certificates. They SHOULD also support matching the certificate identifier with a reverse DNS lookup of the connecting peer, with results cacheable or looked up in advance in case DNS itself is unstable or compromised.
sections.eli5: Both sides show an ID card before talking, and each checks the other's card against a list of friends. Nobody is allowed to use the old, weak locks.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Apart from the TLS rules above, the security considerations of the related documents, especially IODEF (RFC 5070) and RID (RFC 6545), apply and are incorporated by reference.

Following BCP 56 (RFC 3205), IANA assigned port 4590/tcp to RID with the service name "RID over HTTP/TLS". The RFC reasons that a substantially new service, which should be controlled at the network border differently than ordinary HTTP/TLS, needs its own port.
sections.eli5: All the safety rules of the other two documents still count here too. RID also got its own door number, so network guards can treat it differently from normal web traffic.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 6046
sections.content:
This RFC obsoletes RFC 6046 and moves it to Historic status. The changes are:

  • The document is now Standards Track.
  • It refers to the updated RID specification, RFC 6545.
  • Language on HTTP/1.1 and TCP ports for RID transport is clarified.
  • The RID-Callback-Token header is added, so RID replies can be matched during callback regardless of the content of the underlying RID message.
  • The minimum required TLS version rises to 1.1 and the minimum recommended version to 1.2.
  • PKI language is clarified and updated to refer to RFC 6125.
sections.eli5: This is the improved edition of an older rulebook. It adds claim tickets for slow answers and bans the oldest, weakest locks.
